Hi all,




Just in response to the email below re: cost points:



a) Cost of the application for PG stepping down temporarily as Lead Sols on Lead Cases.
Unless I am mistaken, a formal application to amend the GLO should not be required to remove Pogust Goodhead as Lead Solicitors. If all parties agree, this can be dealt with by way of consent order and submitted for court approval prior to the PTR. In that
 scenario, any adverse costs for amending the GLO would be minimal, if any.

If an application has to be made because the Defendants will not agree by consent, then the normal costs consequences apply i.e. costs follow the event. If the Defendants unreasonably refuse, we should not be liable for their adverse costs. If, however, they
 say they will only agree by consent if PG pays their costs incurred since Thursday’s announcement, those costs ought to be minimal. As with any offer for adverse costs, we would need to take client instructions, but the costs exposure can be mitigated if the
 application is made sooner rather than later.



b) Ability to recover common costs as Lead Sols.

Common costs are recoverable inter partes by reference to the approved costs budgets. The default position under each GLO is that Lead Solicitors conduct the common costs work. However, the cost-sharing provisions allow such work to be delegated (with prior
 authorisation) to a Non-Lead Solicitor. This is what has already occurred in Ford, Renault-Nissan, and Citroën-Peugeot with Milberg London LLP.

For example, the Mercedes GLO [43] states:
With the exception of such preparation for and attendance at meetings of the Claimants' Solicitors Group as is reasonably required, no further work in relation to the Common Issues shall be undertaken by any legal representative other than the members of the
 Steering Committee, their servants or agents 
unless authorised in advance by the Steering Committee; and no liability for Common Costs in relation to such work in the absence of such authorisation shall arise between the Claimants or between the parties.

This may therefore require an update to clients to explain that the default position has changed; however, we can also explain the mechanism under the GLO, which permits Non-Lead firms to conduct common work when authorised.



c) CFA deductions.

I do not think the judgment in Julia Mazur v Charles Russell Speechlys LLP [2025] EWHC 2341 (KB) should cause concern. Paralegal work is recoverable in costs provided that:

(a) it does not involve conducting “reserved legal activities” independently;
(b) it is supervised by an authorised individual; and
(c) it is reasonable and proportionate in nature and amount.

None of our paralegals conduct reserved legal activities within the meaning of section 12(1) of the Legal Services Act 2007. These activities are limited to:



the exercise of a right of audience;


the conduct of litigation (issuing a claim form, signing statements of truth, filing a defence/response, etc.);


reserved instrument activities (e.g. drafting a transfer of land, completing registration documents for the Land Registry);


probate activities;


notarial activities; or


administration of oaths.


Accordingly, PG stepping down as Lead Solicitors does not prevent the firm from being instructed under the GLO to conduct common work and does not impact the level of CFA deductions that may be applied to client damages.

Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to
 you, as I’m sure you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where
 we are. What is important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting
 my notice demonstrates that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation,
 I'm more than happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm;
 and ii) to address on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure
 the clients are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to
 those deadlines, the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)



As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added
 complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall Pan-NOx CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO)
 for permission to be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the
 CROs, is necessarily extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they
 are not in the CRO i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the
 applications / witness statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall,
 as it should come at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date
 that will allow me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that
 I leave the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients,
 it would appear the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale
 of importance considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and,
 I believe, will have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The
 obvious link is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this
 in a professional and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe
 it is in the clients best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance
 with my professional and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed
 to this. As such, I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make
 bookings into the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I
 can then claim back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer
 be in the employ of the firm).


This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance
 where the firm has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.


Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial.
 This rental starts on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead
 booking me into hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.


Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally
 and the recover the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.


I look forward to hearing from you, and should you require anything further, please let me know.

Michael

Please see attached a draft of the letter with my suggested amendments and comments.


 


The most important point here is to make sure that what is said about PG’s funding agreements is accurate and not misleading by omission, because anything that isn’t quite right (or a relevant funding arrangement
 not included) will doubtless be seized on down the line.


 


On the ATE assumptions, my views are as follows (and I know these are shared by Simon):


 



We think that future costs for ADR and Experts should be included in the relevant expenditure calculations. Despite not having been assessed by the court yet, those costs would be incurred
 within the relevant period and therefore will be taken into account when assessing of sufficiency of cover. It would be reasonable at this stage to take the Claimants’ offers against those phases as the starting point for what we say is required, but we must
 recognise that leaving those phases out altogether isn’t going to be defensible before the court. So if para 9a and 9b are to go into the letter (and I can see they may be needed for now if the position on sufficiency of cover is to be maintained) we need
 to accept internally that there will need to be movement on that point (and additional cover) if the position on ATE sufficiency is to be maintained before the court.



 




Similarly, we don’t think there is a strong case for downgrading the % of incurred costs by 10%. Again, if this is to go into the letter we ought to treat it internally as a holding position
 while you look to increase cover.


 


We agree that it is not sensible to disclose in the letter that you are looking to increase cover. Most importantly, that essentially amounts to a concession that what you have is insufficient - and additionally,
 as you point out, you may not be able to secure further cover and we don’t want to box ourselves in.


 


I hope that helps. I am around tomorrow morning if needed until around 1pm.

Thanks Sarah, I’ll adjust to take account of that point about % of incurred costs (but will wait for any other comments before doing so).
 
On the Post-July point:
We are 100% on the same page for the scenario if Cs win the PDD trial.
On scenario B (Cs lose PDD), I think the difference come from these two parts of your list below:

Quantum trial will not happen – when we were discussing this earlier in the year pre-PTR, I recall there was
 hesitation in the group about whether it would be as simple as this (or at least whether it was something we were happy to express this in these absolute terms). That’s where my concerns about the case for ‘full’ cover originate from. If we are now able (and
 happy) to say that an adverse outcome in the PDD trial would mean in practice that the T3 trial was immediately vacated that’s fine, but my understanding from previous chats was that it might not be as simple as this, and/or there could be outcomes which were
 effectively losses but which were not strictly fatal to the T3 trial going ahead? If we can’t assert that T3 would go away immediately upon an adverse PDD judgment, then we can’t say the costs will either, and so that’s where the difference of approach arises
 from I think.Quantum PTR, Trial Prep and Trial Phases will ever be incurred – if the T3 trial does get vacated at the end
 of July 2026, then you are correct that the Trial phase shouldn’t be incurred (unless some small part is used for a form of ‘consequentials’ but:


The PTR is due to be held in July 2026 I think ([47] of Quantum directions) so there’s a very real chance those costs are incurred, even if the hearing
 itself gets used for something else at the last minute; andGiven the trial starts in October with summer in between, I anticipate at least some of the trial prep costs will be incurred before the end of July. I
 expect some tranches of brief will be incurred, and there will also be at least some solicitor work (eg I can see there are trial bundle deadlines in July at [52]-[55]).

So, I think the key question is whether or not we can say with confidence that if Cs lose (/ receive an adverse costs order in) T2, that is likely to mean that the T3 trial gets abandoned at the
 end of July 2026. I’m in PG/LDs hands on that. If that’s something we can say, then yes, I can see the argument that there is unlikely to be a set of circumstances which lead to needing cover for the ‘full’ T3 period. If it is more complicated that that, T3
 might still go ahead, that’s where we get the potential for a greater today ATE requirement.
But even if it is correct and the T3 trial would get immediately vacated, I don’t think it would necessarily mean that none of Quantum PTR or Trial Prep are incurred. I expect at least some of each
 would be incurred (and TP is obviously a sizeable sum).
 
Thanks
Simon

Hi Anna,




Following on from yesterday and the calls with LD, a few things we would suggest are raised with Martyn. Firstly, it is important to say the Case Leads and PG team are wildly committed to this trial. That should not be in question.
 However, the AA (the executed version of which the case leads were only sent at 9.22AM this morning), which has been referred to in Court documents and has been incepted without the consent of those persons it applies to (either expressly in the case of the
 Case Leads or, as far as the wider team is concerned, by implication), causes concern. Additionally, the case leads have also raised serious concerns about the staff's  mental health that are yet to be addressed by the firm.




The AA was incepted with little to no visibility or consideration for how it will practically work (as is clear given Martyn's explanation in ​the call on 8 October was substantially different to our understanding of what it means,
 a view which we consider you, also on that call, shared). We need further clarity on the AA. This is true for both for the Case Leads, and the PG staff who will be indirectly subject to it - by way of taking instructions from the Case Leads who are under the
 supervision of Leigh Day.  As we have already told you, there is a real risk of the substantive PG team being entirely alienated by this agreement. These concerns were evidently ignored (including our concerns over the mental health and well-being of the staff)
 given it was executed without further recourse to us.  It also remains unclear what, if any, interaction LD is to have with the wider PG team, if they are not subject to the AA (and therefore direction and supervision), and whether, given this, the PG team
 would need to revert to one of the Case Leads for every interaction, instruction, discussion had with the LD team. An obvious example of this is the trial bundle/logistics workstreams which have largely been left between the excellent PG associates and LD
 with limited input from the case leads. It is fair to say the PG team carries that workstream and LD are unprepared to take it on. Similarly with Opus and issues at this morning's hearing. 




It would be helpful for an explanation, and for the physical AA, to be sent out to the wider PG team along with some practical guidance about what it means. It would be inappropriate for the Case Leads to do this given: i) we
 haven’t agreed to the AA; and ii) it has been incepted against our consent.




It would be helpful if the explanation covered:





what LD expect from the PG team  - do they simply expect the PG teams to "do what they're told, when they're told", or is there still going to be a collaborative
 approach (the former seems more likely given how things have happened over the last few days); 


how the "do what they're told, when they're told" works - or, indeed wider interaction works, in circumstances where the team isn't caught by the agreement. Will they need to take each instruction and run it past a Case Lead?

what happens in circumstances where the PG teams disagree with LDs position on decisions? How does this get resolved between the firms? We stress this is not a hypothetical. Aside from wider case strategy
 we have had immediate differences in opinion last week in terms of costs, with decisions being made and taken without reference to PG. This impacts all claimants, and, of course PG's clients. Further, in terms of wider points, as we have pointed out, LD do
 not have clients on some of the secondary or ALGLO cases, all of which are bound by the PDD trial judgment. It is easy to anticipate a diversion of opinion/strategy as the PDD trial develops which could impact PG only cases/clients and for which, under the
 AA the Case Leads cannot wear two hats.  

how working practices are going to change, both outwardly to the Ds and Court etc, and whether a working group should be set up to standardise approach e.g. do all things on the PG SharePoint move across
 to LD - what is the timeframe, how is it co-ordinated? Whilst an administrative concern this does have significance in terms of sheer volume and also maintaining/transferring admin rights for links particularly where the Defendants and the Court already retain
 access. 

How does it work for the costs team? 





Each of these, along with sight of the AA, will go some way to helping the PG staff understand the agreement they are now working under and hopefully to stop the wheels from falling off. This will also assist in answering questions
 the Case Leads have, but it will not, we doubt, satisfy any regulatory concerns we have, and we request again the Board's complete answer to our note of 05.10.2025 (under cover of email of Sarah Bingham). To date we have not had any answer from you. 




On this point, we thought it helpful to also compile a few outstanding requests from our end to you / the Board. We should also say thank you again for speaking to Alicia and arranging the call with the employment solicitor. While
 we hope this will assist in clarifying the position in terms of whether this AA can be imposed upon us and not contravene our employment contracts, it will not be able to answer any of our regulatory concerns (in respect of the AA and wider regulatory concerns).
 These really can only be answered by the following: 





the advice from BWKC or any other counsel on the AA. This is especially true where many of the concerns we have raised overlap with those in the HSFK letter - including the regulatory position for us
 as lawyers, and the position on client consent. We still have not consented to the AA and we all have significant regulatory concerns. In particular we have not seen any advice which contradicts our position that client consent is necessary for the AA.

Re the AA and how strategic decisions are made, a very practical question: in circumstances where LD and PG (either collaboratively or by PG being informed)
 make a decision, do the PG bods have to in turn report these to the Board / AV? Do we have to report where decisions have been made that we do not agree with? What is our internal reporting matrix for issues such as this? 

Will our COLP, in their role as COLP, be giving us sign off on the agreement, in addition to the Counsel advice?

As our COLP is now also a case lead (for Pan NOx and it appears individual cases), is there a delineation of the COLP roles, from the role of case lead,
 and CEO of the firm? How is this safeguarded?





If these questions are not answered to a satisfactory standard, then our regulatory concerns will remain and as regulated persons, we will need to consider our positions and what, if any, further steps we need to take.




Thanks,




Case Leads

Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you,
 as I’m sure you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we
 are. What is important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting
 my notice demonstrates that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation,
 I'm more than happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm;
 and ii) to address on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure
 the clients are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to
 those deadlines, the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall
 Pan-NOx CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for
 permission to be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs,
 is necessarily extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are
 not in the CRO i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications
 / witness statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as
 it should come at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that
 will allow me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave
 the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it

Hi Matt, Ben, (and Anna as I know you have touched base with BJKC), 




I have exchanged emails with the silks on this, and we agree that we need to recall the corro back asap given it contained extracts of amber documents.  That is in breach of CPR 31.22.  I note from your email below that you say that the amber docs have turned
 green.  That’s not accurate: although they turn green after 7 days (only for Cs), this will not always happen if Ds’ object is upheld.  At the moment, they remain amber and subject to the 7-day notice period, and we cannot collaterally use them.  




We think the best way around this is to (i) recall them immediately;  (ii) tell Ds we have done so; and (iii) apologise to Ds to take the sting out of it.  If we don’t then we risk turning Cockerill against us, which is obviously very unwise.  




Ultimately, we need to remember that this is not really our battle to have, even if with think it might help with settlement.

 for the mental health and well-being of our staff. We further flagged that the proposal creates a two-tier structure amongst the wider team, which risks alienating individual members of the staff. Your email worryingly does not address any of those concerns,
 nor does it even mention them. 



We also note that various junior staff within the NOx department have been enlisted to send out correspondence, including on weekends, relating to non-common work and non-PDD
 Trial matters (see, for example, an email from Hannah Varghese at 15.32 on Saturday, 4 October 2025). Requiring the most junior staff to become actively involved in non-common work issues, while on the other hand attempting to assert that “everything we
 have done or are intending to do is with the best interests of our clients as well as our staff in mind first and foremost” is simply unreal. Correspondence of that nature and related to non-common work should be sent by an individual not working on critical
 workstreams.  



Each of the case leads are committed to finding a co-operative solution to the issues that are being raised. That is why we are proactively engaging in discussions and, in aid
 of assisting the firm, why we have continued to raise points so as to avoid the firm falling foul of issues that they may otherwise be presented with, e.g. noting potential additional disclosure obligations re. documents referred to in witness statements.
 You also have said that you “welcome any specific input we wish to contribute”. This is difficult to contemplate as being a genuine offer in circumstances where a) the SL AA was provided by Leigh Day (“LD”), not you nor the Board, despite Pogust
 Goodhead (“PG”) being our employer; and b) where we have previously sought to provide input (e.g. meeting with Alicia Alinia at 18:00 Monday 29 September 2025) and you have not engaged with it. Instead, you have sent us an email that dismisses our concerns
 and informs us that our description of the SL AA is incorrect, while at the same time stating that your intention is for this email to now bring these discussions to a conclusion. This is neither helpful nor is it in the spirit of co-operation.  



For the avoidance of any doubt, we do not consent to the SL AA in its current form. No representations can be made to the Court at the PTR on 6 October that this has been put
 in place and is agreed. To the extent that you and the Board believe you can bind individuals named in the SL AA (or annexes) by virtue of it being a ‘firm decision’ we disagree for reasons set out below. Every individual subject to the agreement either does
 not consent to it (the case leads) or, as far as we are aware, has never seen any version of it and so is unable to have provided consent.  We accept of course, that Counsel can inform the Court (on 6 October or otherwise) that it is being drafted and the
 intention is that it will be put in place in due course.  



If we, as the collective case leads, are to work collaboratively with the Board and you, and HR, to establish how we can move forward amicably, then it requires serious engagement
 from you and the Board, and not a dismissal of our concerns.  



We trust that this email will allow for a more collaborative approach going forward. 



On the points in your email: 


1.                  
Purpose and Effect of the Side Letter 


You explained that PG’s proposed role is intended to operate “exactly as envisaged”
within the existing Pan-NOx AA framework, and that the SL AA will simply implement a delegation of common work from LD to PG personnel. If that were indeed the case, a separate SL AA would not be necessary; indeed, this accords with our own understanding
 that the new arrangement is entirely novel.  



 



You say this agreement is to “ensure that [we] can continue to work as currently on the existing work plans.” Having reviewed the SL AA, it is clear that it goes
 further than the delegation provisions in the Pan-NOx AA, and that is precisely why it requires a standalone agreement. The SL AA imposes materially different terms in at least two key respects: 



 



a.
Formal separation of supervision and control 



The SL AA introduces an unusual structure whereby PG personnel will perform common work solely under the direction of LD, but remain employed and supervised by PG. Indeed, we
 understand that the Board intends for PG personnel to carry out generic/firm-specific work under PG’s direction. This formalises a split between line management and professional control that is not addressed, let alone authorised, in the Pan-NOx AA. That agreement
 permits delegation of work to another firm, not delegation of the supervision of one firm’s employees to another while the employer retains all employment obligations. 



 



b.
Governance over PG’s internal personnel decisions 



The SL AA (via Annex B) requires LD’s consultation and agreement before PG can add or remove PG personnel from common work. That means PG cannot unilaterally deploy or reassign
 its own staff in this litigation without LD’s approval. This imposes external governance over PG’s workforce, a control that is not contemplated in the Pan-NOx AA and which cuts across PG’s autonomy as an employer. 



 



The SL AA changes the status quo in material ways such that it cannot be said that what is being proposed is “exactly what we have all been working under” or that “this will
 not practically change much day to day.”  



 


2.                  
Tension with Employment Contracts 


Because the SL AA goes beyond what is authorised in the Pan-NOx AA, it creates direct tension with the terms of PG employment contracts. You advise that “there will be no
 change to your employment contract” and that “consent by employees is not necessary for PG to execute the agency agreement.” We respectfully disagree. 



Clause 2(b) of the SL AA states that “PG Personnel shall perform such Common Work … solely under the direction of, and reporting solely to, Leigh Day.” This directly conflicts
 with multiple provisions that we presume appear in each individual employee contract: 


 

a.
Duty of obedience and supervision 

Under Clause 4/Duties of the employment contract (which we presume is a standard term of contract for all PG employees), PG employees are contractually required to comply with
 PG’s directions and report to PG line managers. They are to “devote the whole of their time, attention and abilities to the business of the Company.” The SL AA seeks to override that by imposing a structure in which we report solely to LD in respect
 of a major portion of our work, without any formal secondment or variation of contract. 

 

b.
Regulatory oversight 

The split between day-to-day supervision (by LD) and formal employment responsibility (by PG) creates regulatory ambiguity under the SRA Code of Conduct. Who is the supervising
 solicitor? Are there two supervising solicitors, one from Leigh Day and another from PG? Which firm bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with professional standards?  

 

These are not academic questions - they carry regulatory and indemnity implications.  

 

c. Consent and legal clarity 

The arrangement introduces a dual-control model, but without staff consent, proper transparency, or any framework setting out lines of accountability. As PG remains the employer,
 yet LD directs our work in practice, the legal and ethical basis for this arrangement is unclear, particularly when conflicts, confidentiality obligations, or errors arise. 


 


3.                  
Professional Indemnity Insurance Risk 
The SL AA structure also raises serious questions around insurance cover. If PG personnel are performing common
 work solely under LD’s direction (as the SL AA confirms), then it is not clear whose professional indemnity (“PI”) insurance would respond in the event of a professional error. This is in circumstances where PG remains the/our employer and is responsible
 for holding PI cover for its staff. But LD is envisaged as exercising the day to-day control and making the litigation decisions. The SRA expects supervision and insurance liability to be aligned. That is not the case here. 


 



This is not hypothetical. A clear example of this risk occurred this week when LD made a costs offer to the Mercedes Defendants without PG’s knowledge or approval from PG's
 insurer - despite the fact that PG personnel had prepared the underlying work. If that offer proves problematic, it is unclear whether PG or LD (or both) would be liable and, more importantly,
whose insurer would be on risk. That ambiguity creates risk for both firms and undermines the clarity of the delegation framework set out in the Pan-NOx AA. 



 



This is precisely why the Pan-NOx AA structured delegation at the firm level: to avoid splitting supervision and risk in a way that confuses accountability. The SL AA
 unpicks that structure and introduces unnecessary exposure. 



 



We refer you to 17(a) of the PTR skeleton argument filed by Mercedes where the Defendants have drawn the Court’s attention to this issue. 



 


4.                  
Client Consent 


If PG wishes for us and other PG staff to be instructed by, and report solely to, a firm other than PG, then this requires our express consent, and (we believe) the informed
 consent of the clients whom we act on behalf of (which will not only be just the clients of PG, but  may extent to all clients within every GLO if the work is to be Pan-NOx). If PG personnel are to carry out work on those clients’ cases under the direction
 of a different firm, the clients must be told who is supervising that work and must provide informed instructions to that effect. We refer you to Rule 1.4 of the Code of Conduct, which requires solicitors to ensure clients are in a position to make informed
 decisions about their representation. You cannot unilaterally impose this on us, or on any of the PG staff, nor PG’s clients as your email  suggests you can. 
 
You cannot unilaterally impose a change of supervisory firm on your employees or on the clients, as your email equally suggests. The assumption that this arrangement can simply be implemented without individual or client-level engagement is not supported by
 the regulatory framework. This concern is not novel: post our comments in this regard, this is also expressly identified in the skeleton argument filed by Mercedes at paragraph 17(b), where they raise the potential for regulatory impropriety in precisely these
 circumstances. 



Turning to other points specifically raised in your email:  


·               
You note that we are obliged to work our notice periods. Thank you for pointing this out again, although we note it is not consistent with representations that PG has
 made to the Defendants and Court that the timing of our last days are subject to ongoing discussion. You go on to say that once our notice period has expired, we are free to commence working for JLG, should we so choose. Collectively, none of us have informed
 you of our plans post-PG.  

 

·               
You have advised that LD and counsel have approved this solution. Please provide us with this correspondence (including the advice the firm has taken from counsel
 – as originally requested). We note that as per Martyn Day’s email on 3 October at 13.56 that “Alicia has asked that we leave these issues for PG to sort out with the team. We await the outcome of those discussions and so no need for the meeting this afternoon.”
 In circumstances where LD are waiting for PG to “sort out these issues with the team” and that they will “await the outcome”, we fail to understand how LD have approved the solution. 

 

·               
You advise that you are “now interviewing so with time this work-stream will be handed over”. Please explain which work-stream? Does this relate to non-common
 work? 


We repeat that we are keen to try and work together to find a collaborative solution to these issues, not least because of the importance of the upcoming PDD Trial beginning
 in a little over a week’s time and for which we are all deeply invested in and, in truth, where all of this is causing a huge and detrimental distraction. However, it is plain to us that the SL AA is plainly more than a simple delegation mechanism. It alters
 the control and supervision structure, restricts PG’s governance over its own staff, creates clear tension with employment contracts and regulatory obligations, and places work done on behalf of the PG clients under the instruction of an external law firm
 (without any proposal for client consent to be obtained). If there is to be a material change, it needs to be handled transparently and within a proper legal framework. We raise these points constructively and in good faith, with the shared goal of ensuring
 compliance and continuing to act in our clients’ best interests. 



We trust these concerns now demonstrate that the issues raised in the draft SL AA document need to be engaged with, and we look forward to hearing from you on those issues and
 how they can be addressed, such that we can move forward, together.   The Case Leads

Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you,
 as I’m sure you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we
 are. What is important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting
 my notice demonstrates that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation,
 I'm more than happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm;
 and ii) to address on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure
 the clients are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to
 those deadlines, the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall
 Pan-NOx CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for
 permission to be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs,
 is necessarily extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are
 not in the CRO i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications
 / witness statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as
 it should come at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date
 that will allow me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical
 part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms
 as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it
 would appear the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale
 of importance considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe,
 will have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious
 link is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a
 professional and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is
 in the clients best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance
 with my professional and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to
 this. As such, I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings
 into the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then
 claim back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be
 in the employ of the firm).


This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where
 the firm has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.


Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial.
 This rental starts on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead
 booking me into hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.


Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and
 the recover the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.


I look forward to hearing from you, and should you require anything further, please let me know.


Best,


Michael

Thanks Matt. Anna - on the CCom role:





I will need to go back and check (the GLO applications were made in 2023) but I think we will have taken instructions on the applications;

Unknown - I haven't played a role in Vauxhall.

On my cases at least, I provide them with monthly updates. On top of those updates, I will also contact them for instructions on items such as discontinuances or material updates.

On the expert applications, I advised them of the applications, but did not take their instructions on the actual content of the application. The key reason for this was due to the confidential nature of the

Given the material change to the Litigation that us stepping down as Lead Sols will have, and the change in PGs role (and therefore the CComs roles) in the Litigation, this strikes me as a classic time when we need to a) advise them of why we are doing this
 and b) take their instructions on doing so. 




You are right that the relationships with the CComs are less involved than they may be on other Litigations, and that the CComs play a more passive role in the Litigaiton, but we can't just set that to the side. We can't continue to let our clients think we
 are "running" the Litigation when we are not. I think that risks 1.4 COC.




As a bare minimum we need to advise them of a) and long before they hear of it in the press. To actively deny them this information (and to not take instructions) strikes me as a route that we should not consider going down. I suppose we could always run it
 past counsel (maybe Friston?) to get a seal of approval.




There is also a significant cost angle that needs to be considered here in a) the costs that the Ds may seek to recover from us as a result of this application (though I can see the Ds trying to make unjustified hay about it) and b) our foregoing of the ability
 to recover common costs as Lead Sols (accepting LD can permit us to undertake certain work), and the potential liability of the Cs and their ATE position. This may also have an impact on any CFA deduction we later seek to take as we may no longer have a shortfall
 on common costs sufficient for the total permitted deduction. Allying this with the recent decision in
Mazur (on non-qualified staff doing legal work) - something which we need to think very carefully about in terms of individual work - we may find ourselves in a position where recoverability needs re-assessed. Note - I've already flagged this to Jamie
 McF and asked him to do a note for us to consider internally how this may impact us. It's very new judgment that everyone is grappling with. 




The insurers should also be informed of all of this as well though given the Board have been meeting with them, I presume they have kept them up to date with the material changes. 




Happy to discuss further and to continue to work on the draft to progress it as far as we can (although I think it's pretty much there now and we need Board input to advance it further). Let us know what we can do to help. 




Thanks,




Michael
